candidates.topic: Oxford University older than the Aztec Empire
candidates.teaser: A university so old it makes the Aztec Empire look like a startup — wait until you hear this.
candidates.video_title: Oxford Is Older Than the Aztec Empire 🤯
candidates.video_description: Oxford University began teaching in 1096, centuries before the Aztec Empire even existed. This mind-bending timeline fact reshapes how we think about history.
candidates.script: Oxford University was already over 400 years old by the time the Aztec Empire was founded. Teaching began at Oxford around 1096 AD. The Aztecs didn't establish Tenochtitlan until 1325. That means students were sitting exams, writing essays, and debating philosophy in Oxford for four full centuries before the Aztecs even broke ground on their capital city. We tend to imagine ancient civilizations and medieval Europe as happening at the same time — but the timeline is wildly different from what most of us picture. So here's the question: what else in history are you picturing in completely the wrong order?

candidates.teaser: There's a creature swimming in our oceans that's older than trees — and it's still hunting today.
candidates.video_title: Sharks Existed Before Trees Were Invented 🦈
candidates.video_description: Sharks have been on Earth for around 450 million years — long before the first tree ever grew. They survived every single mass extinction event in Earth's history.
candidates.script: Sharks have been swimming in Earth's oceans for roughly 450 million years. Trees? They only appeared about 350 million years ago. That means sharks were already ancient by the time the first tree grew its first leaf. Sharks survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. They survived four other mass extinctions before that. Their basic design was so perfect that evolution barely changed them. While entire ecosystems rose and collapsed around them, sharks just kept hunting. They are genuinely one of the oldest complex predators to ever exist on this planet. So the real question is — if sharks survived everything Earth has thrown at them, what could possibly threaten them now?

candidates.topic: Vending machines kill more people than sharks annually
candidates.teaser: You're statistically more likely to be killed by a snack machine than by a shark — and the numbers don't lie.
candidates.video_title: Vending Machines Kill More People Than Sharks
candidates.video_description: On average, vending machines cause around 13 deaths per year globally, while shark attacks kill far fewer people annually. Your fear of sharks may be completely misplaced.
candidates.script: Every year, vending machines kill more people than sharks do. Globally, around 13 people die annually from vending machines — usually from tipping one over trying to shake out a stuck snack. Shark attacks, despite all the movies and headlines, cause fewer fatalities worldwide per year. Yet almost nobody is afraid of a vending machine. Our brains are wired to fear things that look dramatic and dangerous, not the boring everyday things that are quietly more lethal. Sharks get the horror films and the news coverage. Vending machines just sit there looking innocent. So next time you reach for that stuck bag of chips — maybe step back first. Which everyday object do you think hides a surprising danger?

candidates.topic: The Pacific Ocean is shrinking and the Atlantic is growing
candidates.teaser: One of Earth's oceans is slowly disappearing — and it's been happening your entire life without you noticing.
candidates.video_title: The Pacific Ocean Is Slowly Disappearing 🌊
candidates.video_description: Due to tectonic plate movement, the Pacific Ocean shrinks by a few centimeters every year while the Atlantic Ocean gradually expands. Earth's surface is in constant slow motion.
candidates.script: The Pacific Ocean is shrinking. Right now, as you watch this, it's getting smaller — about a few centimeters every single year. The tectonic plates beneath it are pulling the ocean floor under the surrounding continents in a process called subduction. Meanwhile, the Atlantic Ocean is quietly growing wider at roughly the same rate. It sounds slow, but over millions of years these tiny shifts completely redraw the map of our planet. The ocean you think of as the world's largest has an expiration date written into the geology of Earth itself. Scientists estimate the Pacific could eventually close entirely — in about 300 million years. Does it change how you see a map knowing the oceans themselves are moving?

candidates.topic: Humans glow in the dark with biophotons
candidates.teaser: Your body is literally glowing right now — you just can't see it with the naked eye.
candidates.video_title: Your Body Glows in the Dark — Seriously 💡
candidates.video_description: The human body emits a faint visible light called biophotons, about 1,000 times too dim for our eyes to detect. Japanese researchers captured this glow on camera using ultra-sensitive equipment.
candidates.script: Your body is glowing right now. Not metaphorically — literally emitting visible light. Human skin produces tiny particles of light called biophotons, a faint glow generated by chemical reactions happening inside your cells. It's real, measurable light, not heat — actual photons. Japanese scientists photographed this glow using cameras so sensitive they can detect a single particle of light. The glow is about a thousand times too dim for your eyes to see under normal conditions. Interestingly, the light is strongest around your face in the late afternoon and weakest early in the morning. Your body has its own light cycle. So the question is — if we could see each other's biophoton glow, what do you think we'd look like?
